title: Heat Stress, Hydration, PPE and Emergency Response

content.overview: Heat risk in cultivation is a work-system problem, not a test of toughness. Outdoor and greenhouse heat, high humidity, radiant load, physical work and protective clothing can combine quickly. Prevention requires planning, acclimatization, hydration, recovery, communication and an emergency response that workers can use without delay.

vocabulary.definition: The total heat burden on the body from environment, workload and clothing/PPE.
Physiological adaptation that develops gradually with repeated heat exposure.
A range of heat-related conditions that can progress from early symptoms to a medical emergency.
A shaded, cooled or otherwise appropriate area where workers can reduce heat load.
A work practice in which workers and supervisors watch for signs that a person may not recognize in themselves.

sections.title: Assess heat as conditions change
sections.body: A greenhouse may be acceptable early and hazardous later. Air temperature, humidity, radiant heat, workload, duration and PPE should be reconsidered as the shift or task changes.

sections.title: Acclimatization changes risk
sections.body: New workers, returning workers and people whose heat exposure has changed may be less adapted. Work planning should account for gradual acclimatization rather than assuming prior experience guarantees tolerance.

sections.title: Hydration and recovery must be planned
sections.body: Water, rest and an appropriate recovery area should be available before symptoms appear. Prevention cannot depend only on thirst or on a worker requesting a break after heat strain is already significant.

sections.title: PPE can increase heat burden
sections.body: Chemical or task-specific PPE may reduce evaporative or convective cooling. When PPE is required, schedule, workload and recovery planning should account for the added burden rather than relaxing the protective requirement.

sections.title: Emergency response must be explicit
sections.body: Workers should know who to contact, what symptoms trigger immediate escalation, how to move a person to a safer environment when appropriate and how emergency medical help will be obtained. Serious symptoms are not managed by simply giving water and sending the person back to work.

workedExamples: A greenhouse task is comfortable at 8 a.m. but conditions and solar load rise sharply by noon. The work plan is reassessed rather than carried forward unchanged.
A pesticide-handling task requires protective clothing. The team schedules the task for a lower-heat period and adds recovery planning rather than removing required PPE.
A returning worker begins a high-workload hot shift after weeks away. The supervisor uses a more conservative acclimatization/work plan.
commonMistakes: Using thirst as the only hydration trigger.
Assuming experienced workers cannot develop heat illness.
Using one morning condition reading for an entire shift.
Failing to define who initiates emergency response.
content.practicalApplication: Create a heat-work plan for an outdoor or greenhouse shift. Record expected conditions, workload, required PPE, acclimatization concerns, water/recovery availability, reassessment points, communication method and emergency escalation steps.
content.summary: Heat safety requires active management throughout the shift. Conditions, workload, acclimatization, PPE, hydration, recovery and emergency readiness must be planned together.

blocks.title: The task changed
blocks.setting: A worker planned a light greenhouse scouting task but is reassigned to move heavy containers while wearing required protective clothing as afternoon heat rises.
blocks.prompt: What should happen before the heavier work continues?
options: Nothing; the original plan still applies
Reassess heat risk, workload, PPE burden, recovery and monitoring before continuing
Remove required PPE to offset the workload
Ask the worker to drink extra water and continue
blocks.answer: Reassess heat risk, workload, PPE burden, recovery and monitoring before continuing.
blocks.feedback: Heat plans must reflect actual conditions and workload, not only the original schedule.

blocks.title: Heat-work preflight
blocks.instructions: Build a one-page preflight for a hypothetical hot cultivation shift.
prompts: What work intensity and PPE are expected?
Who may need additional acclimatization protection?
Where are water and recovery areas?

visualNeeds.teachingObjective: Learner sees how radiant load, humidity, workload and PPE can change risk across a shift.
Learner distinguishes prevention, early symptom response and emergency escalation.
